findings.title: Device limit enforcement is racy: check-then-act allows exceeding the configured limit
findings.body: CreateOrUpdateDevice first calls CountDevices and only falls back to updateDevice when count >= deviceLimit, otherwise it performs an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT. This is a classic TOCTOU race: under concurrent anonymous requests (the normal case for a public Grafana instance), many goroutines can observe count < limit simultaneously and all insert new devices, exceeding AnonymousDeviceLimit. The limit is a security/abuse-control feature (bounding anonymous device rows), so silently exceeding it defeats its purpose. The count and insert are not performed in a single transaction or with any locking, so there is no atomicity. A correct implementation would enforce the limit atomically (e.g., conditional INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < limit, or a transaction with locking/serializable isolation), or at minimum treat the limit as best-effort and document it.

findings.title: updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for any device that does not exist or is outside the time window, not only when the limit is reached
findings.body: updateDevice runs an UPDATE ... WHERE device_id = ? AND updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ? and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached whenever RowsAffected == 0. RowsAffected is 0 both when the device does not exist (a brand-new device hitting a full table) and when the device exists but its updated_at is outside the [now-30d, now+1m] window (e.g., an expired device that the periodic cleanup has not yet removed, or clock skew). In both cases the caller (client.go Authenticate) treats ErrDeviceLimitReached as a hard failure and rejects the anonymous request, so legitimate first-time visitors can be denied access even though the device table is not actually full. The error conflates 'device not found / stale' with 'limit reached'; the update path should distinguish these (e.g., fall back to insert when the row is missing, or return a distinct error) instead of failing authentication.

This PR removes the goroutine and the timeout and calls a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...) synchronously with the request context. Two consequences: (1) every anonymous request now pays the latency of a COUNT(*) query plus an INSERT/UPDATE against the database on the critical auth path, adding DB load and latency to all anonymous traffic; (2) when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached (which, per the updateDevice issue, can happen for brand-new devices), Authenticate returns nil, err and the anonymous user is completely denied access — turning a telemetry/abuse-control limit into a full authentication outage for new visitors. In client.go only ErrDeviceLimitReached is treated as fatal, but other callers of TagDevice (and any future callers) now receive errors they did not before, and the local-cache set in tagDeviceUI (line 87) happens before the DB write, so a failed write still marks the device as cached for ~29 minutes, suppressing retries. It never verifies the intended behavior that motivated updateDevice: when the limit is reached, an already-known device should still be updated (its updated_at refreshed) rather than rejected. findings.title: New device_limit setting has no default documentation, no validation, and no sample config entry
findings.body: cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit is read via anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0). There is no validation that the value is non-negative (a negative value silently disables the limit because database.go checks `s.deviceLimit > 0`, which may be intended but is undocumented), no entry in conf/sample.ini or docs describing the setting, and no default.ini documentation of its meaning (max number of anonymous devices tracked in the last 30 days). Since this is a user-facing configuration knob that changes authentication behavior (rejecting anonymous users when reached), it needs documentation and a sane guard (e.g., reject or clamp negative values with a warning) so operators do not misconfigure it.

findings.title: anonymousDeviceLimit typed as `number | undefined` but backend always serializes an int64 (0 when unset)
findings.body: The Go DTO declares `AnonymousDeviceLimit int64 `json:"anonymousDeviceLimit"`` with no omitempty, so the backend always sends a JSON number (0 when the setting is unset/default). The TypeScript type `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined` and the runtime default `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined` imply the field may be absent, but it never is; consumers checking `config.anonymousDeviceLimit === undefined` to detect 'not configured' will never see undefined, they will see 0. The frontend type should be `number` (matching the always-present JSON), or the Go field should be a pointer with omitempty if absence is meaningful. As written the `| undefined` is misleading and any frontend logic branching on undefined is dead code.
